questions.prompt: An op-amp with open-loop gain \(G=2\times10^{4}\) is used in a loop with feedback factor \(f=0.01\). What is the loop gain \(T\)?
questions.explanation:
\(T=G\,f=2\times10^{4}\times0.01=200\).
Because \(T=200\gg1\), the closed-loop gain \(G/(1+T)\approx 1/f=100\) with an error of about \(1/(1+T)=0.5\%\).

questions.prompt: In a non-inverting op-amp amplifier, \(R_2\) runs from the output to the inverting input and \(R_1\) runs from the inverting input to ground. What is the feedback factor f?
options: \(f=\dfrac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}\), the fraction of \(v_{out}\) that the divider returns to the − input
questions.explanation:
The divider feeds \(v_{out}R_1/(R_1+R_2)\) back to the − input, so that is f, and the ideal gain is \(1/f=1+R_2/R_1\).
• \(1+R_2/R_1\) is the ideal closed-loop gain, the inverse of f.
• \(R_2/(R_1+R_2)\) is the fraction dropped across \(R_2\), not the fraction fed back.
• \(R_2/R_1\) is the inverting amplifier's gain magnitude.

questions.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has \(R_1=3\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_2=27\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) around an op-amp with open-loop gain \(A=2000\). What is its actual closed-loop gain?
questions.explanation:
\(f=3/30=0.1\), so the ideal gain is 10 and \(T=Af=200\). Actual gain: \(\dfrac{A}{1+T}=\dfrac{2000}{201}=9.95\), 0.5% below ideal.
• 10 is the ideal \(1/f\).
• 9 is \(R_2/R_1\), the inverting gain magnitude.
• \(2000/(1+0.1)\) adds f instead of the loop gain \(Af\).

questions.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has \(R_1 = 2\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (to ground) and \(R_2 = 38\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (from output to the inverting input). The resistive divider is the feedback network. In the limit of a very large op-amp gain, what is the closed-loop gain \(1/f\)?
questions.explanation:
The divider returns \(f=\dfrac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}=\dfrac{2}{40}=0.05\) of the output to the inverting input. For huge \(G\), the gain is \(1/f=\dfrac{R_1+R_2}{R_1}=1+\dfrac{R_2}{R_1}=1+19=20\).
Common mistake: using \(R_2/R_1=19\) (that is the inverting-amplifier magnitude) or \(R_1/(R_1+R_2)\) (that is \(f\), not \(1/f\)).

questions.prompt: The same amplifier (\(f = 0.05\)) is built with an op-amp whose finite gain is \(G = 1000\). What is the actual closed-loop gain?
questions.explanation:
\(G_{closed}=\dfrac{G}{1+Gf}=\dfrac{1000}{1+1000\cdot0.05}=\dfrac{1000}{51}=19.61\).
This is about 2% below the ideal value of 20, because \(Gf=50\) is large but not infinite.

questions.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has \(R_1=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_2=49\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and an op-amp gain \(A=10^{4}\). What is its loop gain \(T\)?
questions.explanation:
The feedback factor is \(f=\dfrac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}=\dfrac{1}{50}=0.02\). The loop gain is \(T=A\,f=10^4\times0.02=200\).
Common mistake: using \(T=A\) (forgetting that the divider throws away 98% of the signal on its way back) or \(T=A\,R_2/R_1\).

questions.prompt: An inverting amplifier with \(R_S=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_F=9\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) uses an op-amp with gain \(A=10^4\). Breaking the loop at the op-amp's output, what is the magnitude of the loop gain?
options: \(1000\), since the voltage returning to \(V^-\) is \(R_S/(R_S+R_F)=0.1\) of \(v_o\), and \(T=A\cdot0.1\)
questions.explanation:
With \(v_s=0\), the output voltage reaches the inverting node through the divider \(R_S\) (to ground) and \(R_F\): \(V^-=v_o\dfrac{R_S}{R_S+R_F}=0.1\,v_o\) (reader Eq. 17.36–17.37, \(f=\dfrac{R_S}{R_S+R_F}\)). The op-amp multiplies \(V^-\) by \(-A\), so \(|T|=A f=1000\).
The OTHER divider ratio, \(g=\dfrac{R_F}{R_S+R_F}=0.9\), is how the INPUT reaches \(V^-\); it matters for the gain but not for the loop gain.
Reader note: Eq. 17.36 is correct as printed (\(V^-=v_o\frac{R_S}{R_S+R_F}+v_s\frac{R_F}{R_S+R_F}\)); students often swap the two weights.

questions.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has \(f=0.01\) (ideal gain 100). The gain error must be at most 0.05%. What minimum op-amp gain \(A\) is required?
questions.explanation:
The fractional error is \(\dfrac{1}{1+T}\le 0.0005\), so \(1+T\ge2000\) and \(T\ge1999\).
Since \(T=A f\), \(A=\dfrac{T}{f}=\dfrac{1999}{0.01}=1.999\times10^{5}\), about \(2\times10^5\).
Note the gotcha: the required \(A\) depends on \(f\). A larger \(f\) (smaller closed-loop gain) needs proportionally less \(A\).

questions.prompt: An inverting amplifier has input resistor \(R_1=2\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and feedback resistor \(R_2=18\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), with an op-amp of gain \(A=5000\). What is its loop gain T?
questions.explanation:
With the input source zeroed, \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) still form a divider from the output back to the − input: \(f=R_1/(R_1+R_2)=0.1\). So \(T=Af=500\), even though the ideal gain is \(-R_2/R_1=-9\), not \(-10\).
• \(A/9\approx556\) wrongly takes f as the inverse of the closed-loop gain.
• 5000 assumes the whole output is fed back.
• \(A\cdot R_2/(R_1+R_2)=4500\) uses the wrong resistor in the divider.

questions.prompt: Preview of feedback errors. A non-inverting amplifier uses \(R_1=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_2=99\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) around an op-amp with finite gain \(G=10^5\). The ideal gain is \(1/f\). By what percentage is the actual gain below the ideal value?
questions.explanation:
\(f=\dfrac{1}{100}=0.01\), so the ideal gain is \(1/f=100\). The actual gain is \(\dfrac{10^5}{1+10^5\cdot0.01}=\dfrac{10^5}{1001}=99.9\).
Error \(=\dfrac{100-99.9}{100}=0.0999\%\), which equals \(\dfrac{1}{1+T}=\dfrac{1}{1001}\). A later skill ('static and dynamic errors') studies exactly this gain error and how it grows when \(T\) falls.

questions.prompt: Preview of the gain-bandwidth trade-off. An op-amp has \(A(jf)=\dfrac{10^5}{1+jf/10\ \mathrm{Hz}}\) and is used as a non-inverting amplifier with \(f=1/20\). What is the closed-loop −3 dB bandwidth, in kHz?
questions.explanation:
Closing the loop moves the pole up by \(1+T_0=1+10^5/20=5001\): \(f_{-3dB}=10\ \mathrm{Hz}\times5001=50.0\ \mathrm{kHz}\), and the DC gain falls to about 20. Gain times bandwidth stays near \(10^6\ \mathrm{Hz}\).
• 10 Hz is the open-loop bandwidth.
• 1 MHz is the unity-gain frequency, where the gain is 1, not 20.
• 500 kHz divides the GBW by 2 instead of 20.
questions.figure_alt: Open-loop op-amp Bode magnitude: 100 dB to 10 Hz, then falling 20 dB per decade to 0 dB at 1 MHz.

questions.prompt: Preview of feedback and impedance. An op-amp with open-loop output resistance \(R_o=100\ \Omega\) is used in a non-inverting amplifier with loop gain \(T=1000\). What is the closed-loop output resistance, approximately?
options: About \(0.1\ \Omega\): sensing the output voltage divides \(R_o\) by \(1+T\)
questions.explanation:
The loop samples the output voltage and fights any change in it, so a load current produces \(1+T\) times less output change: \(R_{out}=R_o/(1+T)\approx0.1\ \Omega\). The impedance skill covers when feedback divides an impedance and when it multiplies one.
• Feedback does change impedances; that is one of its main uses.
• Multiplication happens for the input resistance of this configuration, not its output resistance.
• It is never exactly zero with finite T.
